title: Rehearse the agentified day

proposed_identity.status: historical precedent only; L13-L16 purpose-specific rights pending

presenter_passages.passage_exact: It is Friday at Harbor Learning Circle. Morgan opens a paper brief, not a live dashboard. The preparation agent's job was to compare three cleared course inputs and draft a Session Option Brief. The first line says prepared, not sent.
The six beats are useful because they make those boundaries routine.

offscreen_narration.text:
A second line says staffing is unconfirmed. A third says a research proposal has not run. Morgan's day is not about clearing every row. It is about spending judgment where a decision can change what happens next.

The Six-Beat Day begins with a brief. What was prepared? What needs a human? What may be worth learning? Harbor's answer is short: one paper brief was drafted; staffing and spend need decisions; a layout question may deserve a test. The brief must carry receipts and uncertainty. If it reads like an endless task list, the system has handed burden back to Morgan.

Second, route. The staffing question belongs to the program lead and team, not to the preparation agent. A proposed spend belongs in a separate budget decision. The research question belongs to Morgan as owner of the brief format. Route each item to a named person, with a deadline or review window where appropriate. Routing an item to a queue without an owner is a way to lose it politely.

Third, review. Morgan reads the brief beside its source-status summary and trace template. One course source is stale for the proposed month. The agent's draft sounds confident anyway. Morgan marks the claim unsupported and keeps the staffing hold in place. Fourth, approve. There is nothing to approve for a team proposal today. Morgan may approve a correction to the paper draft for later review, but that is not approval to book a session, spend money, or send an announcement.

Fifth, recover. Suppose the paper handoff is incomplete: the draft lacks its source-status field. Morgan does not fill the gap by guessing. The recovery choice is to return the brief for a corrected paper draft, preserve the earlier version, and record why. There is no automatic retry or provider call. Sixth, learn. The repeated missing source-status field could become a memory proposal: require that field in future briefs. It stays a proposal until Morgan reviews its source, scope, and expiry. One bad draft does not write policy by itself.

At day's end, Morgan asks one uncomfortable question: what did I approve that I should have questioned? In this rehearsal the answer is a paper correction, and Morgan can revisit it. The staffing, spend, research, and memory decisions remain distinct. Pause and name the beat in your workflow where a human is most likely to approve too quickly.

Write a Six-Beat Day brief for your workflow. For each beat, name the item, evidence, owner, safe action, and stop condition. Make one thing fail. Show how the operator recovers without hiding the original version. Mark any lesson as a memory proposal rather than an approved rule. Close with the question you would ask after a busy day. Use a fictional or approved example. Do not use private operational data, open a live account, import a trace, or contact a person.

Save revision fifteen as a draft. Harbor's day ends with a held brief, a visible correction path, and decisions still owned by people.

gates: purpose-specific L13-L16 look and voice approval

visual clipping, label collision or unreadable captions
